events.fact: Kentucky was admitted to the Union as the fifteenth state, the first carved from the western frontier beyond the Appalachians.
Mortally wounded aboard the USS Chesapeake off Boston, Captain James Lawrence gave the order 'Don't give up the ship' in the frigate's losing battle against HMS Shannon.

block: On June 1, 1792, Kentucky entered the Union as the fifteenth state, drawing the rough settlements of the western frontier under the ordered government of the young Republic. On the same day in 1813, Captain James Lawrence, dying of his wounds aboard the USS Chesapeake near Boston, charged his crew with words that outlived him, 'Don't give up the ship.' An Obedient citizen takes both lessons to heart, submitting himself to the lawful order that binds a free people and holding fast to his post until duty is discharged, trusting the God who appoints every man his station.

events.fact: Jack Jouett rode through the night some forty miles from Cuckoo Tavern to Charlottesville to warn Governor Thomas Jefferson and the Virginia legislature of Tarleton's approaching cavalry, saving them from capture.
Astronaut Edward H. White II became the first American to walk in space, stepping outside the Gemini 4 capsule for twenty-three minutes.

block: On June 3, 1781, Jack Jouett spurred his horse through the dark Virginia woods for forty miles to warn Governor Thomas Jefferson and the assembled legislature that Banastre Tarleton's dragoons were coming, and his upright watchfulness spared the leaders of the Revolution from British capture. On the same day in 1965, Edward H. White II opened the hatch of Gemini 4 and became the first American to walk in space, venturing alone into the void for twenty-three minutes above the earth. An Upright citizen keeps watch as Jouett did and presses boldly into the unknown as White did, doing what honor and duty require whether the eyes of men are upon him or no, for God sees in the dark as in the light.

events.fact: More than 156,000 American, British, and Canadian troops stormed the beaches of Normandy on D-Day, the largest amphibious invasion in history, beginning the liberation of Western Europe.
United States Marines launched their assault at Belleau Wood in France, a brutal three-week battle that became one of the Corps' most storied stands of the First World War.

block: On June 6, 1944, more than 156,000 Allied soldiers crossed a stormy Channel and threw themselves against the fortified beaches of Normandy, and through the carnage of that single morning the liberation of a captive continent began. On the same day in 1918, United States Marines opened their attack at Belleau Wood, where in the first day they suffered more casualties than the Corps had borne in its first one hundred forty-three years, yet would not be driven back. A Steadfast citizen looks to those ranks of plain men who advanced into withering fire and held their ground, learning to stand fast in his own appointed trial and to commit the outcome to the God of battles who numbers every fallen son.

events.fact: Richard Henry Lee introduced his resolution in the Continental Congress declaring that the united colonies 'are, and of right ought to be, free and independent States,' the formal motion that led to the Declaration of Independence.
The four-day Battle of Midway concluded with a decisive American naval victory over Japan, sinking four enemy carriers and turning the tide of the war in the Pacific.

block: On June 7, 1776, Richard Henry Lee rose in the Continental Congress and moved that the united colonies 'are, and of right ought to be, free and independent States,' setting his name and his honor to a plain and upright declaration of principle before any sword had secured it. On the same day in 1942, the Battle of Midway closed in a stunning American victory, four enemy carriers sunk and the momentum of the Pacific war wrested from a stronger foe. An Upright citizen, like Lee, will state the truth plainly and stake himself upon it, and like the sailors at Midway will hold the line against long odds, confident that the God of justice upholds the cause that is right.

events.fact: Representative James Madison rose in the House of Representatives to introduce the amendments that would become the Bill of Rights.
Andrew Jackson, seventh President of the United States and hero of the Battle of New Orleans, died at his home, the Hermitage, in Tennessee.

block: On June 8, 1789, James Madison stood before a skeptical House of Representatives and introduced the amendments that would become the Bill of Rights, persevering against colleagues who thought the matter a distraction until the liberties of the people were secured in writing. On the same day in 1845, Andrew Jackson, seventh President and the iron-willed victor of New Orleans, died at the Hermitage in Tennessee at the age of seventy-eight. A Steadfast citizen presses his good labor through to completion as Madison did with the Bill of Rights, and faces his own appointed end with the resolve Jackson showed, having spent his strength in service and leaving the rest to the God who keeps and judges every soul.

events.fact: Rhode Island colonists led by Abraham Whipple and John Brown rowed out by night and burned the grounded British revenue schooner HMS Gaspee in Narragansett Bay, an early act of open resistance before the Revolution.
King George II's privy council finalized the royal charter establishing the colony of Georgia under the trusteeship of James Oglethorpe, the last of the thirteen British colonies in America.

block: On June 9, 1772, a band of Rhode Island men rowed out under cover of darkness and burned the British revenue schooner Gaspee where she lay aground in Narragansett Bay, standing firm against a Crown they judged to have overreached its lawful bounds. On the same day in 1732, King George II's privy council finalized the charter for Georgia, founding the last of the thirteen colonies under James Oglethorpe as a refuge for the worthy poor. A Steadfast citizen holds his ground against injustice as those Narragansett men did, and labors patiently to build something lasting as Oglethorpe did on that southern frontier, trusting the providence of God to establish the work of faithful hands.

events.fact: United States Marines landed at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, in the Spanish-American War, seizing the harbor in the Corps' first major action of the conflict.
Benjamin Franklin is traditionally remembered to have flown a kite in a thunderstorm near Philadelphia, drawing electric charge from the clouds and proving that lightning is electricity.

block: On June 10, 1898, the First Battalion of United States Marines waded ashore at Guantanamo Bay and took the harbor from Spanish forces, obeying their orders in the Corps' first significant battle of the war. On that same day in 1752, by long tradition, Benjamin Franklin raised a kite into a Philadelphia thunderstorm and drew sparks from the clouds, obediently submitting his bold idea to the test of nature and learning that lightning and electricity are one. An Obedient citizen follows his orders into hard duty as those Marines did, and bends his mind to the laws God has written into His creation as Franklin did, knowing that true mastery comes only to the man who first submits.

events.fact: The Continental Congress appointed the Committee of Five, Thomas Jefferson, John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Roger Sherman, and Robert Livingston, to draft the Declaration of Independence.
John Wayne, the actor whose Western and war films made him an enduring emblem of American grit, died in Los Angeles at the age of seventy-two.

block: On June 11, 1776, the Continental Congress named the Committee of Five and charged it to draft a declaration of independence, and the men obediently took up a task whose weight no one could yet measure. On the same day in 1979, John Wayne died in California, an actor whose rugged portrayals of soldiers and frontiersmen long stood in the American imagination for plain courage and steady duty. An Obedient citizen shoulders the assignment placed before him as Jefferson and his fellows did, and honors in his own bearing the quiet, dutiful manhood that Wayne's heroes embodied, answering the call of his hour as unto God.

events.fact: The Fifth Virginia Convention unanimously adopted George Mason's Virginia Declaration of Rights, the first such bill of rights in America and a model for the federal one to come.
President Ronald Reagan stood at the Brandenburg Gate in West Berlin and challenged the Soviet leader, 'Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!'

block: On June 12, 1776, the Virginia Convention unanimously adopted George Mason's Declaration of Rights, setting down in firm language that all men are by nature free and possessed of rights no government may take, a charter that would shape the nation's own Bill of Rights. On the same day in 1987, President Ronald Reagan stood before the Brandenburg Gate and steadfastly demanded that the Soviet leader 'tear down this wall,' refusing to soften his words before tyranny. A Steadfast citizen plants himself upon enduring truth as Mason did and speaks it boldly in the face of power as Reagan did, holding the line for liberty in the conviction that God has made men to be free.

events.fact: Winfield Scott, who would serve as Commanding General of the United States Army for twenty years and earn the name 'the Grand Old Man of the Army,' was born near Petersburg, Virginia.
New York City gave Charles Lindbergh a ticker-tape parade before some four million people, honoring his solo nonstop flight across the Atlantic from New York to Paris.

block: On June 13, 1786, Winfield Scott was born in Virginia, a soldier who would serve his country faithfully under the flag for more than half a century and command its army through war and peace as the Grand Old Man of the Army. On the same day in 1927, four million New Yorkers lined the streets to shower Charles Lindbergh with a ticker-tape parade, honoring a young airman who had kept faith with a daring promise and flown alone across the Atlantic to Paris. A Trustworthy citizen earns such honor as these men did, by long fidelity to his duty and by making good on what he sets out to do, that others may rely on his word as on a thing tested before God.

events.fact: The Second Continental Congress adopted the Flag Resolution, establishing the Stars and Stripes of thirteen red and white stripes and thirteen white stars as the flag of the United States, the origin of Flag Day.
The Continental Congress voted to establish the Continental Army, placing the colonial militias under a single national command, the birthday of the United States Army.

block: On June 14, 1777, the Continental Congress adopted the Flag Resolution, decreeing thirteen stripes and thirteen stars upon a field of blue, and so gave a struggling people the banner under which their sons would march and die. On the same day in 1775, that same Congress had voted the Continental Army into being, gathering the scattered militias under one command and founding the army that endures to this day. A Steadfast citizen reverences the colors his fathers raised and the long line of soldiers who carried them, resolving to stand under that standard with the same constancy, and lifting his eyes above the flag to the God whose providence raised the nation it represents.

events.fact: Arkansas was admitted to the Union as the twenty-fifth state, signed into law by President Andrew Jackson.
Charles Goodyear received the patent for vulcanized rubber, the durable material born of years of stubborn experiment that would transform American industry.

block: On June 15, 1836, Arkansas joined the Union as the twenty-fifth state, another commonwealth of the frontier brought under the ordered government of the Republic. On the same day in 1844, Charles Goodyear at last secured the patent for vulcanized rubber, the fruit of years of dogged labor and stinging failure that nearly ruined him before it remade an industry. A Steadfast citizen perseveres as Goodyear did through long discouragement, and takes his place faithfully within the lawful order of his nation as Arkansas did within the Union, knowing that God honors the patient toil of honest hands.

events.fact: Abraham Lincoln delivered his 'House Divided' speech in Springfield, Illinois, on accepting the Republican nomination for the United States Senate, declaring that a house divided against itself cannot stand.
The Ford Motor Company was incorporated in Detroit by Henry Ford and a small group of investors, the enterprise that would put the nation on wheels.

block: On June 16, 1858, Abraham Lincoln told the Republicans gathered at Springfield that 'a house divided against itself cannot stand,' borrowing the words of Christ to warn a fracturing nation and standing firm on that hard truth though it cost him votes. On the same day in 1903, Henry Ford and a handful of backers incorporated the Ford Motor Company in Detroit, a venture that would reward years of perseverance by setting a whole people in motion. A Steadfast citizen speaks the difficult truth without flinching as Lincoln did, and labors on at his calling through doubt and setback as Ford did, anchored in the God who does not change.

events.fact: President James Madison signed the declaration of war against Great Britain, beginning the War of 1812, the young nation's second war for its independence and honor.
Aboard the Space Shuttle Challenger, Sally Ride became the first American woman in space, helping deploy satellites and conduct experiments on the six-day mission.

block: On June 18, 1812, President James Madison signed the declaration of war on Great Britain, and a barely-tested Republic resolved to defend its sailors and its sovereignty against the greatest navy on earth. On the same day in 1983, Sally Ride rode the Challenger into orbit as the first American woman in space, steadily carrying out her duties through six days aloft. A Steadfast citizen stands his ground for his nation's honor as that young Republic did, and presses faithfully into demanding work whatever the danger, resting in the God who upholds those who venture much in a worthy cause.

events.fact: The Continental Congress adopted the Great Seal of the United States, bearing the eagle and the motto E pluribus unum, 'Out of Many, One,' after six years of deliberation.
West Virginia was admitted to the Union as the thirty-fifth state, formed from the loyal western counties of Virginia during the Civil War.

block: On June 20, 1782, after six years of patient deliberation, the Continental Congress adopted the Great Seal of the United States, its eagle clutching the motto E pluribus unum, 'Out of Many, One,' a steadfast emblem of a people made one. On the same day in 1863, West Virginia entered the Union as the thirty-fifth state, its mountain counties having stood by the Union when their mother state seceded. A Steadfast citizen holds fast to the union of his people as that seal proclaims and as those loyal mountaineers proved, refusing to be torn from his commitments and trusting the God who binds many into one.

events.fact: New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify the United States Constitution, reaching the number required to put the new government into effect.
Cyrus McCormick, a devout Virginian, received the patent for his mechanical reaper, an invention that multiplied the harvest and transformed American agriculture.

block: On June 21, 1788, New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify the Constitution, and with that vote the document at last took force and the new American government came into being. On the same day in 1834, Cyrus McCormick, a man of earnest Christian faith, patented the mechanical reaper, an instrument that would let one farmer harvest what had taken many and help feed a growing nation. A Steadfast citizen upholds the constitutional order so firmly secured that day, and applies himself to honest, fruitful industry as McCormick did, believing that diligent work and lawful self-government are alike a stewardship before God.

events.fact: President Franklin Roosevelt signed the Servicemen's Readjustment Act, the G.I. Bill, providing returning World War II veterans with funds for education, housing, and a new start in civilian life.
The British warship HMS Leopard fired upon and boarded the USS Chesapeake off the Virginia coast to seize sailors, an outrage against American sovereignty that helped lead to the War of 1812.

block: On June 22, 1944, President Franklin Roosevelt signed the G.I. Bill, the nation keeping faith with the millions of servicemen who had answered its call by opening to them the schoolhouse and the family home. On the same day in 1807, the British frigate Leopard fired on the USS Chesapeake off Virginia and dragged off her sailors, a humiliation that the young Republic was bound in honor to answer. An Obedient citizen honors the duty a nation owes those who serve it and the duty a man owes his country's flag, submitting himself to the bonds of mutual loyalty that, under God, hold a people together.

events.fact: William Penn concluded his treaty with Tamanend and the Lenape at Shackamaxon, a covenant of peace remembered by Voltaire as the only treaty never sworn to and never broken.
Cherokee leader Brigadier General Stand Watie surrendered at Doaksville, the last Confederate general in the field to lay down arms, ending the Civil War's last command.

block: On June 23, 1683, William Penn met the Lenape chief Tamanend beneath the elms at Shackamaxon and bound himself to a treaty of peace so faithfully honored that Voltaire called it the only one never sworn to and never broken. On the same day in 1865, the Cherokee general Stand Watie surrendered the last Confederate command in the field at Doaksville, keeping his word to lay down his arms once the cause was lost. A Steadfast citizen keeps his covenants as Penn kept his and submits to honorable terms as Watie did, holding that a man's word, once given, is a sacred thing he must keep before the God who keeps faith with His own.

events.fact: The explorer John Cabot, sailing under the English flag aboard the Matthew, made landfall on the North American coast, the first European to reach the mainland since the Norse.
The Soviet Union began its blockade of West Berlin, cutting off the city's land routes and prompting the American-led Berlin Airlift that would sustain its people through the winter.

block: On June 24, 1497, John Cabot brought the little ship Matthew to the North American coast and planted the English flag, opening the continent that would one day cradle a new nation. On the same day in 1948, the Soviet Union sealed off West Berlin, and rather than abandon two million people the United States and its allies answered with an airlift that fed the city from the sky. A Steadfast citizen ventures boldly into the unknown as Cabot did and refuses to abandon those entrusted to him as the airmen of Berlin did not, persevering against great odds in the strength God supplies.

events.fact: At the Battle of the Little Bighorn in Montana Territory, Lieutenant Colonel George Custer and over two hundred soldiers of the Seventh Cavalry were overwhelmed and killed.
North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel and invaded South Korea, beginning the Korean War, into which American troops were soon committed to repel the aggression.

block: On June 25, 1876, George Custer led the Seventh Cavalry into disaster at the Little Bighorn, where he and more than two hundred of his men were surrounded and slain, a grim reminder that pride and miscalculation can undo even seasoned soldiers. On the same day in 1950, North Korean armies poured across the 38th parallel, and Americans were soon called to stand against the invasion in a hard and distant war. A Steadfast citizen learns sober humility from the fall at Little Bighorn and firm resolve from the men who held the line in Korea, standing fast against evil while trusting outcomes to the sovereign God who rules over the rise and fall of armies.

events.fact: Delegates of fifty nations signed the Charter of the United Nations in San Francisco, pledging to work for peace among the nations after the Second World War.
The first American troops of the American Expeditionary Force landed in France at Saint-Nazaire, the vanguard of the doughboys who would help turn the First World War.

block: On June 26, 1945, the representatives of fifty nations signed the United Nations Charter in San Francisco, pledging themselves to seek peace among peoples weary of war. On the same day in 1917, the first American soldiers of the Expeditionary Force stepped ashore at Saint-Nazaire in France, the green vanguard of the doughboys who would soon help break the long deadlock of the Great War. A Steadfast citizen commits himself to a worthy cause and sees it through, whether laboring patiently for peace or answering the trumpet of war, holding his post in the confidence that God governs the affairs of nations and rewards the faithful.

events.fact: At the Battle of Sullivan's Island near Charleston, Colonel William Moultrie and his small garrison in a fort of palmetto logs repelled the British fleet, saving the city in the war's first decisive American victory in the South.

At the Battle of Monmouth in New Jersey, Washington's Continental Army stood toe to toe with British regulars in scorching heat, and Mary Hays, remembered as Molly Pitcher, manned a cannon when her husband fell.

block: On June 28, 1776, Colonel William Moultrie and a handful of South Carolinians held their fort of soft palmetto logs against the broadsides of the British fleet, and their stubborn defense saved Charleston in the first great American victory of the southern war. On the same day in 1778, Washington's army traded blows with British regulars at Monmouth in blistering heat, where Mary Hays carried water and then stepped to a cannon when her husband was struck down. An Obedient citizen stands his ground under fire as Moultrie's men did and takes up the fallen man's burden as Molly Pitcher did, faithful to his orders and his comrades, and trusting his life to the God who gives courage to the dutiful.

events.fact: President Dwight Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act, launching the 41,000-mile Interstate Highway System that would knit the country together.
The British Parliament passed the Townshend Acts, taxing glass, paint, paper, and tea in the colonies and stiffening the American resistance that would grow into revolution.

block: On June 29, 1956, President Dwight Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act, setting in motion the vast Interstate system, a labor of decades that would bind the far corners of the nation with a single network of roads. On the same day in 1767, Parliament passed the Townshend Acts to tax the colonies without their consent, and Americans answered with a steadfast refusal that hardened over the years into a fight for liberty. A Steadfast citizen gives himself to building things that outlast him as Eisenhower's road-builders did, and stands firm against unjust impositions as the colonists did, persevering in the long work and the long struggle alike under the eye of God.

events.fact: President Abraham Lincoln signed the Yosemite Grant, setting aside the Yosemite Valley and the Mariposa Grove to be preserved for public use, the first federal act to protect scenic wilderness.
President Theodore Roosevelt signed the Pure Food and Drug Act, requiring honest labeling and clean handling in the nation's food and medicine.

block: On June 30, 1864, in the midst of the Civil War, Abraham Lincoln signed the Yosemite Grant, setting aside the valley and its great trees to be kept unspoiled for the people, the seed of the national parks to come. On the same day in 1906, Theodore Roosevelt signed the Pure Food and Drug Act, demanding honesty in the labeling of food and medicine and protecting families from the swindler's wares. An Obedient citizen submits himself to the duties of stewardship Lincoln honored, guarding the good land entrusted to him, and to the call for honest dealing Roosevelt enforced, answering in his own affairs to the God who requires truth in the inward parts.
